# Independent audit: finite global cuts add actual boundary speeds

Audited source: `candidate 85a041ec649c5375`, Sections 1–6. The actual-body obstruction in `candidate d9792f1ce8a8f405` was retained as a separate comparison.

**Result: PASS.** No repair identified. This is a genuine finite closure theorem for the specified global supporting-cut class. It does not assert that all compatible velocities belong to that class, topological closure, a positive payment, or an exchange of moving-cap quantifiers.

## 1. Baseline and zero augmentation

The affine support majorants extend from the original integer fibers to their full convex hull, because the base coordinate enters each plane affinely. Thus each proposed inequality has the original body as its zero-parameter feasible body. Joint convexity of each field in the physical variables makes every new cut convex.

Adding the continuous support majorant based at every occupied p with zero field imposes only inequalities already valid on the original body. It changes neither the actual eroded set nor any existing speed. At base z, the choice p=z gives a zero-slack plane for every normal, so every augmented action has a nonempty active index set. This is essential; without it an action with zero speed could prevent the product index set from being active at all.

The invoked bounded continuous support slopes are justified by the fixed finite constraint matrix and nonempty feasible polyhedra. This is the previously established support-slope lemma, not a new continuity assertion for changing constraint normals.

## 2. Product construction and first speeds

The composite slack is exactly the sum of the component slacks with strictly positive baseline coefficients. Since all component slacks are nonnegative, it vanishes exactly when every chosen component slack vanishes. The baseline coefficients need not equal the desired speed coefficients. Keeping them positive even when some desired coefficients vanish preserves the equivalence.

The active choices form a Cartesian product of finite nonempty sets. For nonnegative desired coefficients, the maximum of the summed field is the sum of the individual maxima. Consequently the asserted speed sum follows at each regular original boundary point once the usual radial speed formula is established. No pairing of two different points of a flat facet enters this maximization.

## 3. Actual compatibility and nonsmooth radial proof

Uniform boundedness of the finitely many tuple fields on the compact original fibers and sphere gives a common O(ε) inner homothety. Its support loss is at least the maximum additional field cost in every direction. This proves positive original fibers and ensures a uniform radial domination bound.

At a regular boundary point, every old active plane has the unique original unit normal. Its cut inequality gives the lower radial-speed bound. For the upper bound, an inwardly moved endpoint lies in the old interior, so a new cut must be active. Finite tuples and compact normals give a convergent subsequence. The old support slack and the baseline slack are individually nonnegative; their O(ε) sum therefore forces both to zero at the limit. The limiting normal is the unique old normal. Dropping the nonnegative old slack from the exact active equation gives the matching upper bound. There is no assumption that the active-contact indicator itself is continuous.

Almost-everywhere uniqueness of convex-body normals and radial integration now give the volume derivative. The d=1 endpoint interpretation is correct. Convexity of the new ambient intersection enforces every anchored compatibility condition exactly, rather than merely to first order. The optional rational perpendicular thickening preserves all integer fibers; it is correctly not asserted to lie in a previously fixed ambient body.

## 4. Fixed-cap losses

The three inward selector statuses are correct. A proper cutting plane meets the convex boundary in surface measure zero; otherwise it would be a supporting plane, contrary to properness. Every other radial boundary point has a fixed cap status on its sufficiently thin inward layer. A whole-fiber closed cut, including the inside support and pure-base boundary cases, takes every removed point. An outside supporting trace takes none of the removed d-volume. These conventions also handle d=1.

The same dominated radial argument therefore integrates each fixed selector against the actual summed speed. Every fixed-cap and total loss is the stated nonnegative linear combination. A finite list gives a common little-o bound simply by taking the maximum of finitely many individual remainders. No uniformity over moving halfspaces is asserted or needed.

## 5. Quantifier and scope checks

The resulting response set is an algebraic cone under finite nonnegative combinations. This is not a claim of topological closure for arbitrary sequences of cut fields or unbounded slopes. The finite closed-cover descent corollary retains the full covering and strict-slack hypotheses.

Supporting-cap derivatives with independent cap motions contain branch expressions that are not linear in the joint motion. The source explicitly stops short of linearizing those expressions or swapping direction, menu, and allocation choices. It also distinguishes a prescribed seed credit from the total source cost after all actions are added.

The mechanism is thus new relative to the failed Minkowski interpolation route: it adds the cut fields while constructing new baseline support planes, then forms one actual convex intersection. The earlier square example, whose Minkowski average has speed |x| instead of 1, does not obstruct this different construction.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
